title: Round 1 · Decode CNH Q2 2026
story: Actual CNH results for the quarter ended June 30, 2026. Published August 3. Reported figures stay fixed to their source.

questions.prompt: In CNH reporting, Industrial Activities excludes which business?
questions.explanation: Separate the equipment business from customer and dealer financing when reading margin and cash.
questions.discussion: Which results should a plant staffing proposal be measured against?

valueConnection.why: Separating equipment operations from financing makes the right margin and cash measures easier to use.

questions.prompt: Industrial adjusted EBIT margin moved from 5.6% to 4.0% in Q2. How many basis points did it fall?
questions.explanation: 1 percentage point equals 100 basis points. A margin decline is not the same as a decline in sales.
questions.discussion: Which controllable plant costs can protect margin at the current production schedule?

valueConnection.why: Expressing the margin change in basis points gives the team one clear way to discuss performance.

questions.prompt: CNH Agriculture sales rose 1%, while adjusted EBIT fell 35%. What should you examine?
questions.explanation: Revenue growth can coexist with weaker profit. Use the EBIT bridge to locate the pressure before proposing actions.
questions.discussion: Which variance needs a Commercial, Manufacturing, Purchasing, or HR response?

valueConnection.why: Understanding the profit bridge helps Commercial, Manufacturing, Purchasing, Finance, and HR work on the same business problem.

questions.prompt: CNH Industrial FCF was +$150m in Q2, but −$439m for H1. Which statement is correct?
options: Q2 erased the H1 cash outflow
Q2 was positive; H1 remained negative
H1 excludes the positive Q2 cash result
questions.explanation: Quarter and year-to-date measures answer different questions. Check both before calling the cash position healthy.
questions.discussion: Does a proposed action improve earnings, cash, or both, and when?

valueConnection.why: Keeping quarter and year-to-date cash separate makes the financial position clearer before a decision.

questions.prompt: Q2 North American tractor demand above 140 HP fell 17%. This is a measure of:
questions.explanation: Industry demand is a market signal. It is not a CNH plant schedule or a company sales measure.
questions.discussion: What additional order, retail, and channel evidence would justify a schedule change?

valueConnection.why: Reading the market signal alongside orders and retail demand helps us plan around what customers actually need.

title: Round 2 · Commodities & the Ag Cycle
story: Real USDA and CNH observations. USDA prices are 2026/27 season-average forecasts published September 11, 2026; they are not today's futures quotes.

questions.prompt: USDA's September corn forecast is $4.80/bu for 2026/27. What kind of price is this?
options: The price received by every corn grower
questions.explanation: A seasonal forecast cannot replace a contract-specific futures quote or a local cash bid.
questions.discussion: What price and cost measures best represent the farmers served by our product line?

valueConnection.why: Distinguishing a forecast from a market quote makes a complex commodity signal clearer and more useful.

questions.prompt: USDA forecasts nominal net cash farm income up 0.4%, but down 2.5% after inflation. What is the better reading?
options: Every crop farmer has the same result
questions.explanation: Separate dollar growth from purchasing power and sector totals from the economics of individual customers.
questions.discussion: Which customer segments have the cash, financing capacity, and need to replace equipment?

valueConnection.why: Understanding real purchasing power helps us anticipate the equipment decisions farmers can afford.

questions.prompt: Crop prices rise, but yields fall and fertilizer costs rise. Can you conclude farmers have more equipment-buying capacity?
options: No; check revenue, costs, and liquidity together
No; lower yields alone decide buying capacity
Yes; nominal crop prices measure purchasing power
questions.explanation: Price × saleable yield drives revenue. Input cost, debt service, cash, and timing determine how much reaches an equipment decision.
questions.discussion: What would we need to know before translating a commodity rally into a production ramp?

valueConnection.why: Looking at yield, costs, and liquidity together starts with the farmer’s actual business needs.

questions.prompt: If CNH wholesale shipments rise while dealer retail sales stay flat, what should you check first?
options: Whether wholesale growth proves stronger farmer demand
Whether staffing should rise with wholesale shipments
Whether reported revenue rose with wholesale shipments
questions.explanation: Wholesale moves equipment into the dealer channel; retail moves it to the end customer. Compare both before treating shipments as demand recovery.
questions.discussion: Which product families show genuine end-customer demand rather than channel loading?

valueConnection.why: Checking end-customer demand helps us serve farmers instead of treating dealer shipments alone as customer success.

questions.prompt: CNH's Q2 presentation says cycle indicators improved but recovery was not yet underway. What follows?
options: Commit to a full ramp now
Treat improved indicators as confirmed orders
Use wholesale shipments as the sole ramp trigger
questions.explanation: Readiness work can begin before a schedule increase. The size and timing of a ramp still need current demand evidence.
questions.discussion: Which signals would cause the team to activate, delay, or stop a ramp?

valueConnection.why: Commercial, Operations, Finance, and HR can prepare the recovery together using shared demand signals.

title: Round 3 · Production & Skills
story: Equipment-manufacturing decisions. These prompts teach operating principles; they do not claim to describe conditions at any CNH plant. Use your own demand, skills, quality, and supplier evidence in the discussion.

questions.prompt: Final test is the bottleneck; assembly has spare capacity. Which staffing action best increases shippable output?
options: Move assembly operators into test before qualification
questions.explanation: Staff the constraint. Adding people elsewhere may build work in process without increasing completed machines.
questions.discussion: Which role limits your plant's output, and how long does qualification take?

valueConnection.why: Developing qualified skills at the constraint invests in people and helps them contribute to reliable output.

questions.prompt: Production falls while fixed factory cost stays unchanged. What happens to fixed cost per unit?
options: It stays constant with the factory's total cost
It rises only if wages increase
questions.explanation: Fewer units carry the same fixed cost. That pressure needs a cost and schedule response; it does not prove that extra inventory is useful.
questions.discussion: Which costs are truly avoidable during down weeks, and which remain?

valueConnection.why: Making fixed cost per unit visible helps the team understand the tradeoff and choose a clear response.

questions.prompt: Dealer sell-through is weak. Why avoid building extra units purely to improve absorption?
options: Unsold units release cash when production finishes
Better absorption guarantees stronger cash flow
Inventory ties up cash and can add discount risk
Wholesale shipments prove machines sold to farmers
questions.explanation: Align the plan with credible demand. A favorable unit-cost metric can conceal a worse cash or inventory outcome.
questions.discussion: How are retail demand, wholesale shipments, and dealer inventory reconciled in the production plan?

valueConnection.why: Matching production to genuine customer demand supports the right equipment availability without loading the channel.

questions.prompt: Orders recover. Which evidence best supports a production ramp?
options: Qualified skills, materials, and good-unit capacity
questions.explanation: A name on the roster is not a qualified hour at the right process. Check the constraint, coverage, quality, and parts together.
questions.discussion: What skill, onboarding, attendance, or supplier limit could block the promised ramp?

valueConnection.why: A credible ramp brings together qualified people, materials, quality, and the production plan.

questions.prompt: During a downcycle, what is the best cross-training priority?
options: Spread training evenly across all operations
Skills needed at the next likely constraint
Use course attendance as proof of readiness
questions.explanation: Prioritize coverage that changes executable capacity. Include training lead time and quality requirements.
questions.discussion: What capability can we build now that would shorten a future ramp?

valueConnection.why: Using a downcycle to develop useful skills invests in people’s growth and future opportunities.

title: Round 4 · CBS, Cost & Cash
story: Published CNH Business System vocabulary and the real Agriculture EBIT bridge, combined with practical manufacturing finance decisions.

questions.prompt: In published CNH material, CBS stands for:
questions.explanation: CNH links CBS with daily management, strategy deployment, and kaizen. For HR, connect capability to operating results.
questions.discussion: Which daily measure connects a workforce action to quality, delivery, or cost?

valueConnection.why: Daily management and continuous improvement connect our capabilities to better quality, delivery, and cost.

questions.prompt: In CNH's Q2 Agriculture EBIT bridge, which item was the largest negative movement?
questions.explanation: The bridge shows Volume & Mix at −$102m, versus a +$53m pricing offset. Prioritize the driver rather than treating every variance equally.
questions.discussion: How should staffing flexibility reflect a volume and product-mix change?

valueConnection.why: Focusing on the largest profit driver turns a detailed bridge into a clear business priority.

questions.prompt: An hourly wage increase affects plant product cost. What else belongs in the staffing economics?
options: Benefits, productivity, overtime, scrap, and rework
Hiring cost instead of ongoing productivity
questions.explanation: Evaluate cost per good unit and total cash impact. Manufacturing labor and corporate labor can appear in different financial lines.
questions.discussion: Which workforce option has the lowest total cost for the required quality and output?

valueConnection.why: Judging staffing by good output, quality, and total cost supports better performance than wages alone.

questions.prompt: A training investment relieves the production bottleneck. What makes the business case stronger?
options: Credible good-unit gain and measured cost/cash benefit
Savings based on everyone who attended
questions.explanation: Tie qualified coverage to good output, avoided overtime or rework, and timing. Ask Finance to validate benefits rather than counting participation as ROI.
questions.discussion: Which benefit can be observed after qualification, and who owns the baseline?

valueConnection.why: HR, Operations, and Finance can agree on the training baseline and validate the benefit together.

questions.prompt: A plan reduces rework and work in process without hurting shipments. Which benefit should Finance test?
options: Lower trapped inventory cash and conversion cost
Higher revenue from rework hours eliminated
Labor savings equal to the full WIP reduction
Cash release equal to the entire WIP balance
questions.explanation: Less work in process can release working capital; less rework can lower cost. Confirm both with the controller because accounting and cash timing differ.
questions.discussion: How will we measure cost reduction separately from cash release?

valueConnection.why: Reducing rework and improving flow advances quality and performance while freeing cash for the business.
